Levering a propolis-stuck lid free with the flat of a hive tool, one hand braced firm on the box below while the tool turns slowly until the seal gives with a soft crack.
Easing a frame up out of the box by its lugs, both hands steady and level, lifting it clear of the top bars in one smooth unhurried rise.
Setting a lifted honey super down across an upturned lid on the grass, lowering it gently until it rests square and level and settles still.
Sliding a drawn frame back down into place between its neighbours, guiding it by the lugs until it settles flush with the rest at the bottom of the box.
Prising two propolis-stuck boxes apart with the hive tool worked along each face in turn, both palms pressing outward until the bond releases evenly.
Squeezing two slow breaths of smoke from the bellows low across the top bars, the puff drifting down between the frames in a soft rolling billow.
Feeding a loose handful of dry grass into the smoker's canister, pressing it down gently with two fingers before fitting the lid back into place.
Sweeping bees carefully off a frame face with a soft goose-feather brush, the stroke long and even so the bees lift and drift rather than scatter.
Tipping a full frame slowly forward so a cluster of bees at the lower corner walks back down the wood and drops quietly into the box below.
Drawing a warmed knife steadily down the face of a frame so the cut caps peel away in one long pale sheet, curling into the tray beneath.
Turning the extractor crank in a long, even rhythm, the other hand resting flat on the lid to feel the drum spin true and steady.
Ladling honey through a fine strainer into a wide-mouthed jar, tipping the ladle slowly so the stream stays thin and the foam stays behind in the cloth.
Scraping wax scraps off the bench edge into a bucket with the broad side of the hive tool, gathering each curl with a short patient stroke.
Holding a plain box up beneath a hanging swarm cluster and giving the branch one short, firm, downward shake so the mass drops cleanly inside.
Spreading a clean white sheet out flat on the grass beneath a low swarm, smoothing the corners down with both palms until it lies flat and taut.
Crouching low to watch a loose line of bees walk up the sheet toward the box's entrance, the line moving steadily in single file across the cloth.
Clamping a bare frame on the bench and threading fine wire through each small hole in turn, pulling the wire snug between fingers before moving to the next.
Pressing a sheet of foundation down into a wired frame with both thumbs working outward from the centre until every edge seats flat against the wood.
Painting a hive body with a wide brush held in a steady grip, drawing one long even stroke from top to bottom and then lifting the brush cleanly away.
Floating a flat cork on a saucer of water set beside the hive stand, nudging it to the centre with one fingertip so it sits level.
Reaching up to wedge a flat stone firmly onto a hive lid, pressing it down with the heel of the hand until it feels solid and immovable.
Crouching right down level with the landing board, chin near the knees, watching the steady coming and going a few inches from the entrance.
Holding a jar of honey up between both hands and turning it slowly, looking straight through the amber depth to the light on the far side.
Standing perfectly still with both arms lowered and hands open at the sides while bees stream past on either side in their outbound line.
Cupping an empty piece of comb in both palms and holding it close to look into the open cells one by one, turning it by small degrees.
